sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the data of the GenAI Credit Memo Assistant (CMA, model identifier MDL-20, model version 1.0): the knowledge sources retrieved at inference time, the retrieval index built from them, and the evaluation data sets used to design and test the application. CMA drafts selected sections of credit memos for corporate obligors (legal persons) in the Netherlands and Belgium for the Bank's credit analysts; it is used by Corporate Credit Analysis in annual reviews and new credit applications. CMA has no development data set in the sense of a statistical model, because the foundation model is a third-party model that the Bank neither trains nor fine-tunes; MRM agreed on 3 July 2026 that the RDS template of MRM-STD-021 Annex A is used with a GenAI adaptation, in which the knowledge sources take the place of the modelling population and the golden set takes the place of the target variable. Template sections that do not apply are retained with the statement "Not applicable" and a justification; added sections follow the last template section of the relevant chapter.

sections.heading: Data governance and ownership
sections.text: The five knowledge sources are mapped to the data domains of the Group Data Catalogue: Credit Documentation (KS-1 credit file archive), Corporate Financials (KS-2 financial spreading platform), Client Reference Data (KS-3 client master data and group structure), Credit Risk (KS-4 approved ratings and limits) and Credit Policy (KS-5 policy corpus). The Model Owner agreed the data quality expectations for the 23 critical data elements of CMA with the Data Owners in data quality agreement DQA-CMA-01 of 12 February 2027. Changes to the definition, source or structure of a knowledge source (for example a new document type in the credit file archive) are approved by the Data Owner and notified to the Model Owner at least 20 business days in advance through the catalogue change workflow. The knowledge sources are listed and owned, and are subject to the data quality controls of chapter 6 and to the access controls of section 4.1.6.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The knowledge index at the reference date 31 March 2027 covers the documents of 2,140 active corporate obligors with a document date from 1 January 2019, comprising 186,400 documents split into 1,941,200 chunks, together with 11,900 spread financial statements and 212 policy documents. The golden set GS-CMA v1.2 comprises 320 evaluation cases drawn from 96 obligors, based on credit memos approved between January 2024 and December 2026, each case consisting of a drafting task for one memo section, the source documents available at the memo date and an SME-written reference answer. The retrieval test set RT-CMA v1.1 contains 250 queries with 1,140 labelled relevant passages, and the prompt development set PD-CMA v1.0 contains 180 cases from 58 other obligors. The out-of-time set OT-CMA v1.0 contains 60 cases from memos approved in the first quarter of 2027.

sections.heading: Choice of the collection window
sections.text: Documents from 2019 onwards are indexed because the annual review of a corporate obligor typically uses the last three to five financial years and the previous credit memos; older documents are rarely relevant and increase the risk of retrieving outdated information. The golden set uses memos from 2024–2026 so that the reference answers reflect the current memo template (introduced in January 2024) and cover a period of rising interest rates and energy costs, which changed the content of the financial analysis sections. The out-of-time set from the first quarter of 2027 tests whether performance is stable on memos written after the golden set was frozen.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: CMA has no default-based target variable. The evaluation target is the SME reference answer for each golden set case, together with statement-level labels: each factual statement in a generated section is labelled as supported, unsupported or contradicted by the sources, each numeric value as correct, incorrect or not verifiable, and each case as requiring an answer or an abstention. Labels are assigned by six senior credit analysts under labelling guideline LG-CMA v1.3 (chapter 9); there is no outcome horizon, because the evaluation concerns the faithfulness of the draft at the time of drafting.

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The lineage of every data element used by CMA is documented in Annex A from the source system and field through the ingestion pipeline to the retrieval index or the prompt, with a reference to the performing pipeline job. KS-1 documents are extracted from the credit document management system (CreditDMS) by the nightly job cma-ingest-docs; KS-2 spreads from the financial spreading platform by cma-ingest-spreads; KS-3 legal entity data, legal form, NACE code and group structure from the client reference data hub; KS-4 the approved rating and limits from the corporate rating system and the corporate lending system at request time; and KS-5 the policy corpus from the policy portal weekly. Intermediate stores are the landing zone, the text extraction store (OCR and layout parsing) and the Azure AI Search index cma-idx-prod, hosted in the Bank's Azure tenant in West Europe. Discarded elements used to construct retained elements (for example the raw OCR text used to build layout-aware chunks) are included in the lineage. Data are ingested fully automatically; the only manual input is the SME labelling of the evaluation sets (section 4.1.7).

sections.heading: KS-1 Credit file archive
sections.text: KS-1 contains the documents in the credit files of the in-scope obligors: audited financial statements and annual reports (38% of documents), management accounts and budgets (17%), previous credit memos (11%), valuation reports (6%), covenant compliance certificates (9%), business plans and investment memoranda (5%) and correspondence and other documents (14%). Only documents with status 'final' in CreditDMS are indexed, so draft or superseded versions are not retrieved. Languages are Dutch (54% of documents), English (41%) and German or French (5%). Documents are converted to text with layout-aware parsing; 6.3% are scanned images processed by OCR, whose quality is checked as described in section 6.1.

sections.heading: KS-2 Financial spreading data
sections.text: KS-2 provides the structured financial statements of each obligor as spread by the credit analysts in the financial spreading platform (11,900 statements for 2,140 obligors, on average 5.6 statements per obligor). Spread values are the authoritative source for all financial figures in the drafts: the numeric-claims guardrail compares every number generated by CMA with these values or with a documented calculation from them. Each spread is linked to the source document in KS-1 from which it was spread, and the four-eyes check of the spreading process (spreader and reviewing analyst) is recorded in the platform.

sections.heading: KS-3 Client reference data
sections.text: KS-3 provides the legal entity name, legal form, Chamber of Commerce (KvK) or Belgian enterprise number, LEI, NACE code, country and group structure of each obligor. The legal form is used as an access gate: CMA can only be invoked for obligors whose legal form is a legal person (for example BV, NV, cooperative, foundation or the Belgian equivalents), so that no sole proprietors, self-employed persons or other natural persons are in scope. Names of directors and ultimate beneficial owners are available in KS-3 for the management and ownership paragraph of the company profile, but personal identifiers of natural persons are not passed to the language model (chapter 7).

sections.heading: KS-4 Ratings and limits and KS-5 policy corpus
sections.text: KS-4 values (approved obligor rating, rating date, approved limits and outstanding exposure) are read at request time from the corporate rating system and the corporate lending system and are inserted into the memo header by the application, not by the language model. KS-5 contains the Credit Risk Policy, 14 sector policies and the credit procedures (212 documents), indexed weekly, which CMA uses only to cite applicable policy requirements, for example sector-specific covenant expectations. Policy documents are versioned in the policy portal, and only the version in force at the drafting date is retrieved.

sections.heading: Ingestion, chunking and embedding pipeline
sections.text: Documents are split into layout-aware chunks of up to 800 tokens with an overlap of 100 tokens; tables are kept whole up to 1,500 tokens and split by row groups above that size, and each chunk carries the obligor identifier, document identifier, document type, document date, page and section heading as metadata. Chunks are embedded with the embedding model text-embedding-3-large (version 1, 3,072 dimensions) deployed in the Bank's Azure OpenAI resource in the EU data zone, and stored with a BM25 keyword index in Azure AI Search. For data received from third parties (annual reports and valuation reports supplied by clients or external valuers), the lineage starts at receipt in CreditDMS and records the supplier, the document type and the receipt date. The chunking, embedding and ranking approach and the number of retrieved passages are documented in MDD §4.4, and the index is rebuilt nightly from the source systems.

sections.heading: Access entitlements and security trimming
sections.text: Every chunk carries the access control list of its source document in CreditDMS, and queries are filtered by the entitlements of the requesting user and by the obligor of the memo being drafted. Testing of the entitlement filtering with test users across the entitlement profiles is planned for April 2027. Documents behind information barriers are excluded from the index.

sections.heading: Manual inputs
sections.text: The only manual inputs are the SME labels and reference answers of the golden set, the retrieval test set, the prompt development set and the out-of-time set, prepared by six senior credit analysts. Label files are version-controlled in the evaluation repository cma-eval, each change requires a merge request approved by the lead labeller, and the lineage in Annex A identifies them explicitly as manual inputs with this control. The labelling process is documented as an expert judgement in data treatment (EJ-CMA-01, chapter 9). No manual data manipulation takes place in the ingestion pipeline and no end-user computing tool is used.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Five exclusions are applied to the knowledge index; each is listed with the number of documents and share of the corpus, and the conclusion of the impact analysis is given in section 5.3. X3: scanned documents with an OCR confidence below 85% (3,240 documents, 1.7%), which are flagged to Credit Administration for re-scanning instead of being indexed. X4: documents with a document date before 1 January 2019 (not ingested; 71,300 documents). X5: duplicates identified by content hash (8,910 documents, 4.6% of ingested documents). No exclusion exceeds 5% of the corpus in any segment except X3 for German-language documents (7.4%), which was approved by the Model Owner on 9 April 2027 and reported to Model Validation – AI.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing information is classified per critical data element in Annex C as missing at random, missing for a structural reason or missing because of a data deficiency. Structural gaps (for example no audited statements for a newly incorporated obligor) are not filled: the system prompt requires CMA to state that the information is not available, and the golden set contains 25 cases requiring such an abstention. Missing spread values caused by a data deficiency (0.8% of statements lack a cash-flow statement spread although the source document contains one) are recorded as deficiency DD-CMA-02 and are not imputed; the numeric guardrail then flags any number that cannot be verified. Outliers in spread values (ratio values outside plausibility ranges, for example interest cover above 1,000) are identified with the same documented rules in the evaluation environment and in production, and are shown to the reviewer as warnings rather than corrected. Reference answers of the golden set are never imputed; cases with incomplete reference answers were returned to the labellers or removed (7 cases removed).

sections.heading: Critical data elements and metadata
sections.text: The 23 critical data elements (CDEs) of CMA are the document text, document type, document date, document status, access control list, obligor identifier, legal form, the 12 spread items used in the financial analysis section, the approved rating and rating date, and the golden set reference answers and labels. Each CDE has a business definition, a technical definition and at least one DQ rule for each applicable dimension (Annex A and rule book DQR-CMA v1.0). Metadata for each element (definition, type and format, permitted values, unit and currency, source, Data Owner, update frequency and classification) are recorded in the Group Data Catalogue, and metadata changes are versioned so that the definition applicable at any date can be retrieved. Where the same concept is defined differently (for example EBITDA as reported by the client and EBITDA as adjusted by the spreading methodology), the spreading definition is used, each is labelled distinctly in the index metadata and the difference is documented in Annex A.

sections.heading: Representativeness of the evaluation sets
sections.text: The golden set was stratified to represent the memos written by Corporate Credit Analysis in 2024–2026 by memo section, sector, obligor size, accounting framework and language. Sector shares in the golden set are within 3 percentage points of the memo population for all eleven sector groups; the shares of memos for obligors reporting under IFRS (27% versus 31%), of English-language source documents (40% versus 41%) and of group structures with more than five entities (22% versus 24%) are comparable. The golden set includes 52 edge cases (restated accounts, IFRS 16 lease effects, going-concern paragraphs, multi-currency groups, conflicting figures between documents), 25 cases requiring abstention and 15 adversarial cases with embedded instructions in source documents. The PSI between the golden set and the 2027 production requests expected from the pilot is 0.05 on memo section and 0.07 on sector. Validity and uniqueness of the evaluation sets were checked: no case appears in more than one set, and no obligor of the golden set is in the prompt development set.

sections.heading: Personal data and fair treatment
sections.text: The credit files contain personal data of natural persons related to the corporate obligors (directors, ultimate beneficial owners, guarantors and contact persons), processed under Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (legitimate interest in credit risk assessment) and Art. 6(1)(c) GDPR for the Bank's credit risk obligations; the processing by CMA is covered by DPIA-2026-207, approved by the Data Protection Officer on 30 October 2026. The PII guardrail masks personal identifiers of natural persons (citizen service numbers, dates of birth, private addresses, IBANs of private accounts and passport numbers) before any text is sent to the language model, and blocks such identifiers in outputs; names and roles of directors and beneficial owners are permitted for the management and ownership paragraph. CMA does not evaluate or classify natural persons: it drafts descriptive and analytical text about corporate obligors, does not score or rate any person, and does not use information on the social behaviour or personal characteristics of directors or owners. The legal-form gate (section 4.1.3) ensures that no creditworthiness assessment of natural persons, self-employed persons or sole proprietors is supported.

sections.heading: Choice of the collection window
sections.text: Documents from 2019 onwards are indexed because the annual review of a corporate obligor typically uses the last three to five financial years and the previous credit memos; older documents are rarely relevant and increase the risk of retrieving outdated information. The golden set uses memos from 2024–2026 so that the reference answers reflect the current memo template (introduced in January 2024) and cover a period of rising interest rates and energy costs, which changed the content of the financial analysis sections. The out-of-time set from the first quarter of 2027 tests whether performance is stable on memos written after the golden set was frozen.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: CMA has no default-based target variable. The evaluation target is the SME reference answer for each golden set case, together with statement-level labels: each factual statement in a generated section is labelled as supported, unsupported or contradicted by the sources, each numeric value as correct, incorrect or not verifiable, and each case as requiring an answer or an abstention. Labels are assigned by six senior credit analysts under labelling guideline LG-CMA v1.3 (chapter 9); there is no outcome horizon, because the evaluation concerns the faithfulness of the draft at the time of drafting.

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The lineage of every data element used by CMA is documented in Annex A from the source system and field through the ingestion pipeline to the retrieval index or the prompt, with a reference to the performing pipeline job. KS-1 documents are extracted from the credit document management system (CreditDMS) by the nightly job cma-ingest-docs; KS-2 spreads from the financial spreading platform by cma-ingest-spreads; KS-3 legal entity data, legal form, NACE code and group structure from the client reference data hub; KS-4 the approved rating and limits from the corporate rating system and the corporate lending system at request time; and KS-5 the policy corpus from the policy portal weekly. Intermediate stores are the landing zone, the text extraction store (OCR and layout parsing) and the Azure AI Search index cma-idx-prod, hosted in the Bank's Azure tenant in West Europe. sections.heading: KS-1 Credit file archive
sections.text: KS-1 contains the documents in the credit files of the in-scope obligors: audited financial statements and annual reports (38% of documents), management accounts and budgets (17%), previous credit memos (11%), valuation reports (6%), covenant compliance certificates (9%), business plans and investment memoranda (5%) and correspondence and other documents (14%). Documents are converted to text with layout-aware parsing; 6.3% are scanned images processed by OCR, whose quality is checked as described in section 6.1.

sections.heading: KS-2 Financial spreading data
sections.text: KS-2 provides the structured financial statements of each obligor as spread by the credit analysts in the financial spreading platform (11,900 statements for 2,140 obligors, on average 5.6 statements per obligor). Spread values are the authoritative source for all financial figures in the drafts: the numeric-claims guardrail compares every number generated by CMA with these values or with a documented calculation from them. Each spread is linked to the source document in KS-1 from which it was spread, and the four-eyes check of the spreading process (spreader and reviewing analyst) is recorded in the platform.

sections.heading: Ingestion, chunking and embedding pipeline
sections.text: Documents are split into layout-aware chunks of up to 800 tokens with an overlap of 100 tokens; tables are kept whole up to 1,500 tokens and split by row groups above that size, and each chunk carries the obligor identifier, document identifier, document type, document date, page and section heading as metadata. Chunks are embedded with the embedding model text-embedding-3-large (version 1, 3,072 dimensions) deployed in the Bank's Azure OpenAI resource in the EU data zone, and stored with a BM25 keyword index in Azure AI Search. For data received from third parties (annual reports and valuation reports supplied by clients or external valuers), the lineage starts at receipt in CreditDMS and records the supplier, the document type and the receipt date. The chunking, embedding and ranking approach and the number of retrieved passages are documented in MDD §4.4, and the index is rebuilt nightly from the source systems.

sections.heading: Access entitlements and security trimming
sections.text: Every chunk carries the access control list of its source document in CreditDMS, and every query is filtered by the entitlements of the requesting user and by the obligor of the memo being drafted, so that retrieval respects the access entitlements of the requesting user. Documents behind information barriers (deal teams with inside information, restricted lists) are excluded from the index altogether (section 4.2). Entitlement filtering was tested with 40 test users across six entitlement profiles; no document outside a user's entitlements was retrieved in 4,800 test queries. The index cannot be queried directly by users; access is only possible through the CMA orchestration service, which authenticates users with the Bank's identity provider.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing information is classified per critical data element in Annex C as missing at random, missing for a structural reason or missing because of a data deficiency. Structural gaps (for example no audited statements for a newly incorporated obligor) are not filled: the system prompt requires CMA to state that the information is not available, and the golden set contains 25 cases requiring such an abstention. Missing spread values caused by a data deficiency (0.8% of statements lack a cash-flow statement spread although the source document contains one) are recorded as deficiency DD-CMA-02 and are not imputed; the numeric guardrail then flags any number that cannot be verified. Outliers in spread values (ratio values outside plausibility ranges, for example interest cover above 1,000) are identified with the same documented rules in the evaluation environment and in production, and are shown to the reviewer as warnings rather than corrected. Reference answers of the golden set are never imputed; cases with incomplete reference answers were returned to the labellers or removed (7 cases removed).

sections.heading: Representativeness of the evaluation sets
sections.text: The golden set was stratified to represent the memos written by Corporate Credit Analysis in 2024–2026 by memo section, sector, obligor size, accounting framework and language. Sector shares in the golden set are within 3 percentage points of the memo population for all eleven sector groups; the shares of memos for obligors reporting under IFRS (27% versus 31%), of English-language source documents (40% versus 41%) and of group structures with more than five entities (22% versus 24%) are comparable. The golden set includes 52 edge cases (restated accounts, IFRS 16 lease effects, going-concern paragraphs, multi-currency groups, conflicting figures between documents), 25 cases requiring abstention and 15 adversarial cases with embedded instructions in source documents. The PSI between the golden set and the 2027 production requests expected from the pilot is 0.05 on memo section and 0.07 on sector. Validity and uniqueness of the evaluation sets were checked: no case appears in more than one set, and no obligor of the golden set is in the prompt development set.

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: The DQ assessment of the evaluation index and the evaluation sets was performed from 22 March to 14 April 2027 and covers completeness, accuracy, consistency and timeliness for every CDE and, where relevant, validity, uniqueness and appropriateness. Completeness: 99.6% of final documents in CreditDMS for in-scope obligors are indexed (record level), and 98.9% of indexed chunks carry all mandatory metadata (attribute level). Accuracy: OCR character accuracy on a sample of 200 scanned pages is 99.1%, and spread values reconcile to the source statements for 99.7% of the 1,200 values sampled. Consistency: the document date, obligor identifier and document type in the index match CreditDMS for 99.9% of documents; timeliness: documents are indexed on the night after their status becomes final (lag of one business day). The assessment concludes that the knowledge sources and evaluation sets are fit for the intended use, and it was signed off by the lead GenAI engineer and the Model Owner on 16 April 2027 before the evaluation index and the golden set were frozen.

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: The Credit Memo Assistant (CMA) is a generative AI application that drafts six sections of the credit memo for corporate obligors (legal persons) in the Netherlands and Belgium: company and group profile, business and market, historical financial analysis, cash flow and debt service capacity, collateral and covenants, and ESG and climate summary. It is intended to reduce the time credit analysts spend on descriptive and analytical drafting in annual reviews and new credit applications (about 2,600 memos per year), and to improve consistency with the memo template. Users are the approximately 140 credit analysts of Corporate Credit Analysis; the drafts are reviewed, edited and approved by the analyst, who remains the author of the memo, and the credit decision is taken by the competent credit authority on the basis of the approved rating and the analyst's memo. CMA has no regulatory use; it is not used for own funds requirements, provisioning, rating assignment or pricing, and its outputs are not sent to customers. The purpose, logic, main inputs, limitations and intended use are described in terms understandable to users, validators and supervisors in this chapter, in chapter 8 and in the user guide CMA-UG v1.0.

sections.heading: AI system assessment and AI Act classification
sections.text: CMA was assessed against the AI system definition of Art. 3(1) AI Act: it is a machine-based system that infers from its input (the drafting task and the retrieved documents) how to generate outputs (text content) that can influence the credit decision process, and it is therefore an AI system; the assessment was documented in the AI Inventory on 15 June 2026. The use case was classified as not high-risk: it supports the analysis of legal persons in corporate lending, which is not a creditworthiness assessment of natural persons under Annex III point 5(b), and no other Annex III area applies; the Art. 6(3) derogation is therefore not relied upon. Natural persons are excluded by design: the legal-form gate prevents use for sole proprietors and self-employed persons (EVD-20-KSD §4.1.3). CMA is subject to the transparency obligations of Art. 50 AI Act: users are informed that they interact with an AI system, and generated text is labelled and marked as AI-generated (section 2.4). The use case involves no practice prohibited under Art. 5 AI Act (no manipulation, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, emotion recognition or biometric categorisation). The AI Governance Office reviewed the classification on 18 November 2026 and again on 21 May 2027 for production use, and the classification is reassessed on every material change to purpose, scope, data or autonomy and at least annually.

sections.heading: Model design
sections.text: CMA consists of six components: (1) the drafting panel in the Credit Workbench, where the analyst selects the obligor and the memo section; (2) the orchestration service, which builds the prompt from the versioned prompt template and the retrieved passages; (3) the retrieval service over the knowledge index (EVD-20-KSD); (4) the foundation model gpt-4.1 accessed through the Bank's Azure OpenAI deployment; (5) the guardrail service with input and output checks; and (6) the audit log. For each memo section, the orchestration service issues three to five retrieval queries defined in the section template, passes the top passages with their source identifiers to the foundation model, and receives a draft in a structured format with a source reference for each paragraph. The guardrail service then runs the grounding check, the numeric-claims check, the PII filter and the content checks before the draft is shown to the analyst. The design separates generated text from system-supplied facts: the approved rating, limits and exposure in the memo header are inserted from the credit systems and cannot be generated or modified by the language model.

sections.heading: Boundaries of intended use
sections.text: The use-case approval defines the boundaries of intended use: CMA drafts descriptive and analytical text for the six memo sections and does not produce a credit decision, a rating, a rating override proposal, a risk assessment conclusion or a recommendation to approve or decline. These boundaries are enforced technically: the memo sections 'Risk assessment and mitigants', 'Rating justification' and 'Recommendation' are not available in the drafting panel, the system prompt prohibits recommendations and judgements on the credit decision, and an out-of-scope classifier blocks requests for such content (block rate 100% on 60 test requests). CMA is used only for corporate lending memos of legal persons in the Netherlands and Belgium; any extension of users, affected persons, data or automation requires a new use-case approval. The model is used only within this approved scope, and no credit decision can be taken on the basis of the CMA draft alone, because the credit process requires the approved rating and the analyst's approved memo.

sections.heading: Human-in-the-loop design and transparency
sections.text: Human oversight is exercised by the credit analyst, who reviews every generated paragraph with its source references and guardrail flags, and accepts, edits or rejects it; a memo cannot be submitted to the credit approval workflow while a paragraph is unreviewed or a red flag is unresolved. Criteria for intervention are defined in the user guide: any unsupported or flagged statement, any figure that cannot be traced to a source, and any content outside the section scope; the analyst can stop generation, regenerate or switch the assistant off for a memo, and the Use Case Owner can suspend the application for all users. The drafting panel informs users at first use and in every session that they interact with an AI system, and every generated paragraph is labelled 'AI-generated draft – Credit Memo Assistant v1.0 – generated on [date]' until the analyst approves it. The label is also written as machine-readable metadata (custom document properties ai_generated=true, application name and generation timestamp) into the memo document in the credit workflow. The credit approver sees an 'AI-assisted' indicator on memo sections drafted with CMA, and the reviewer's approval and edits are recorded in the audit log.

sections.heading: Methodology
sections.text: Four alternatives were assessed against documented criteria (regulatory requirements, data protection, faithfulness to sources, performance on the prompt development set, stability, transparency, cost and implementation effort). (A) An open-weight model fine-tuned on historical memos and hosted on premises: full control, but lower drafting quality in the prototype (groundedness 88.2% on PD-CMA) and a high risk of reproducing outdated memo content. (B) Retrieval-augmented generation with a hosted general-purpose model and strict grounding instructions: groundedness 96.1% on PD-CMA, no training on Bank data and traceable sources. (C) Template-based extraction without free-text generation: fully deterministic but limited to tables and standard phrases, with low time savings (estimated 15% against 45% for B). (D) A vendor credit memo software-as-a-service product: limited configurability of prompts and sources and insufficient documentation for validation at the time of assessment. Alternative B was selected; it is less transparent than C, which is justified by the materially better drafting coverage and is compensated by the additional controls of source references, grounding and numeric checks and mandatory human review.

sections.heading: Prompt design
sections.text: The system prompt (version sp-1.6) states the role and task of the model (drafting a section of a corporate credit memo for review by a credit analyst), the permitted sources (only the passages supplied in the prompt), the required output format (structured paragraphs with a source reference per statement, in the language of the memo), the instruction to answer only from the supplied sources and to state explicitly when information is not available, and the prohibited content (credit recommendations, ratings, judgements on the credit decision, personal opinions, speculation and personal data not in scope). Six section templates (st-1.4 to st-1.6) define for each memo section the retrieval queries, the required sub-headings and the key points expected by the memo template. Prompt variants were compared on the prompt development set; the final prompt reduced unsupported statements from 4.9% to 2.1% of statements compared with the first version, mainly by requiring a source reference per sentence and by explicit abstention instructions. System prompt, section templates, retrieval configuration, guardrail configuration and generation parameters are version-controlled in repository cma-platform and released only through the Bank's change management.

sections.heading: Retrieval design
sections.text: Retrieval uses hybrid search in Azure AI Search, combining BM25 keyword search and vector search on text-embedding-3-large embeddings by reciprocal rank fusion, followed by the semantic re-ranker. Queries are filtered on the obligor of the memo and on the user's entitlements, and restricted to documents with a document date within five years of the drafting date, with the most recent financial statements boosted. The top 8 passages per query are passed to the model, with a maximum of 24 passages per memo section (about 14,000 tokens). Retrieval quality was tested on the retrieval test set RT-CMA v1.1 (250 queries): recall of the relevant passages within the retrieved set (recall@8) is 93.6%, above the 90% minimum of AI-STD-710 §6.3, and 89.1% for German- and French-language documents. Chunking parameters (800 tokens with 100-token overlap) were selected over 400 and 1,200 tokens on the same test set (recall 91.8% and 92.4% respectively).

sections.text: Every generated paragraph includes references to the source passages used (document name, date and page), which are displayed as links next to the paragraph so that the reviewer can verify each statement against the source. This level of explainability is proportionate to a drafting aid whose outputs are reviewed in full by a competent analyst.

sections.text: The generation parameters are temperature 0.2, top_p 1.0, maximum output length 2,500 tokens per section and a fixed response format; the low temperature was chosen to reduce variability and unsupported content, as sensitivity tests showed a hallucination rate of 1.6% at temperature 0.2 against 3.4% at 0.7 on the golden set. All evaluations reported in EVD-20-EVAL were run at these production generation parameters, with the production system prompt, templates and guardrail configuration (configuration release cma-cfg-1.3.0). The parameters are part of the versioned configuration and can only be changed through change management with a regression evaluation. Guardrail thresholds were calibrated on the prompt development set: the grounding check flags statements with a support score below 0.80, which maximised the detection of unsupported statements (recall 94%) at an acceptable flag rate (7.8% of statements).

sections.heading: Guardrails
sections.text: Grounding check: each generated statement is verified against the retrieved passages by the groundedness detection of Azure AI Content Safety and an in-house entailment verifier; unsupported statements are highlighted in red and must be resolved by the reviewer before the draft can be approved. Numeric-claims check: every number in a draft (amounts, ratios, percentages and dates) is parsed and compared with the spread values and retrieved passages, with a tolerance of 0.5% relative for rounded amounts and exact matching for dates; ratios are recomputed with the documented ratio library (24 ratios), and any number that cannot be matched to a source value or a documented calculation is flagged to the reviewer. PII filter: inputs to the language model and outputs are screened for personal identifiers of natural persons (citizen service numbers, dates of birth, private addresses, private IBANs and passport numbers), which are masked in inputs and blocked in outputs, and every detection is logged. Prompt-injection and content checks: user inputs and retrieved passages are screened with Prompt Shields for direct and indirect prompt injection, and outputs with the content filters (medium severity threshold) and the out-of-scope classifier for harmful, discriminatory or out-of-scope content. Thresholds and actions (warn, mask, block) are documented in the guardrail configuration gr-1.3, and their effectiveness was tested in the evaluation (EVD-20-EVAL §10).

sections.heading: Benchmarking
sections.text: CMA was benchmarked against the current manual process and against the alternative foundation models of section 4.2. In the shadow pilot, 12 analysts compared 214 CMA drafts with their own memo sections: 71% of CMA paragraphs were accepted with minor or no edits, 22% were edited substantially and 7% were rejected; drafting time for the six sections fell from a median of 3.9 hours to 2.1 hours per memo. On the golden set, the best alternative model reached groundedness of 95.1% and a hallucination rate of 2.8%, against 96.8% and 1.6% for gpt-4.1; the difference is explained by fewer unsupported statements in long financial tables. The Bank's own outcome testing on its credit files is the basis for the approval; provider benchmarks were used only for pre-selection.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivities of the evaluation metrics were computed on the golden set for the key design parameters. Temperature 0.7 instead of 0.2: hallucination rate 3.4% (+1.8 points) and groundedness 95.2%; top-k 5 instead of 8: completeness −4.3 points; chunk size 400 tokens: groundedness −0.6 points; removal of the abstention instruction: correct abstention falls from 92% to 56%; grounding threshold 0.70 instead of 0.80: detection of unsupported statements falls from 94% to 86%. The labelling guideline (EJ-CMA-01) was tested against the strictest alternative, which reduces groundedness from 96.8% to 95.9%. The results confirm that the chosen parameters are on the conservative side for faithfulness, and that the abstention instruction and the grounding threshold are the most important controls.

sections.heading: Assumptions and limitations
sections.text: The material assumptions are that the knowledge sources are complete and correct for the obligor at the drafting date, that the foundation model behaves in production as in the evaluation at the same pinned version and parameters, that the golden set is representative of production requests, and that analysts review drafts diligently. Each assumption was assessed for plausibility: completeness and correctness are supported by the DQ assessment of the index, model stability by version pinning and repeated runs, representativeness by the stratification of the golden set, and diligent review by the edit and rejection rates observed in the shadow pilot and by the monthly quality review. The main residual risk is automation bias, which is mitigated by mandatory paragraph-level review, visible flags and training.

sections.heading: Production controls and logging
sections.text: Code and configuration are held in repository cma-platform; production uses release cma-app-1.0.0 with configuration release cma-cfg-1.3.0, and each request is executed with the approved versions recorded in the log. Each interaction is logged with user identifier, timestamp, component versions (foundation model version, system prompt, retrieval and guardrail configuration), input, retrieved source identifiers, output, guardrail results and the reviewer's decision and edits; logs are retained for 24 months with access restricted to the technical owner, Model Validation, the AI Governance Office and Internal Audit. If the service is unavailable, analysts draft memos manually; the fallback is logged and does not require approval.

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: The Credit Memo Assistant (CMA) is a generative AI application that drafts six sections of the credit memo for corporate obligors (legal persons) in the Netherlands and Belgium: company and group profile, business and market, historical financial analysis, cash flow and debt service capacity, collateral and covenants, and ESG and climate summary. It is intended to reduce the time credit analysts spend on descriptive and analytical drafting in annual reviews and new credit applications (about 2,600 memos per year), and to improve consistency with the memo template. Users are the approximately 140 credit analysts of Corporate Credit Analysis; the drafts are reviewed, edited and approved by the analyst, who remains the author of the memo, and the credit decision is taken by the competent credit authority on the basis of the approved rating and the analyst's memo. CMA has no regulatory use; it is not used for own funds requirements, provisioning, rating assignment or pricing, and its outputs are not sent to customers. The purpose, logic, main inputs, limitations and intended use are described in terms understandable to users, validators and supervisors in this chapter, in chapter 8 and in the user guide CMA-UG v1.0.

sections.heading: Model design
sections.text: CMA consists of six components: (1) the drafting panel in the Credit Workbench, where the analyst selects the obligor and the memo section; (2) the orchestration service, which builds the prompt from the versioned prompt template and the retrieved passages; (3) the retrieval service over the knowledge index (EVD-20-KSD); (4) the foundation model gpt-4.1 accessed through the Bank's Azure OpenAI deployment; (5) the guardrail service with input and output checks; and (6) the audit log. For each memo section, the orchestration service issues three to five retrieval queries defined in the section template, passes the top passages with their source identifiers to the foundation model, and receives a draft in a structured format with a source reference for each paragraph. The guardrail service then runs the grounding check, the numeric-claims check, the PII filter and the content checks before the draft is shown to the analyst. The design separates generated text from system-supplied facts: the approved rating, limits and exposure in the memo header are inserted from the credit systems and cannot be generated or modified by the language model.

sections.heading: Boundaries of intended use
sections.text: The use-case approval defines the boundaries of intended use: CMA drafts descriptive and analytical text for the six memo sections and does not produce a credit decision, a rating, a rating override proposal, a risk assessment conclusion or a recommendation to approve or decline. These boundaries are enforced technically: the memo sections 'Risk assessment and mitigants', 'Rating justification' and 'Recommendation' are not available in the drafting panel, the system prompt prohibits recommendations and judgements on the credit decision, and an out-of-scope classifier blocks requests for such content (block rate 100% on 60 test requests). CMA is used only for corporate lending memos of legal persons in the Netherlands and Belgium; any extension of users, affected persons, data or automation requires a new use-case approval. The model is used only within this approved scope, and no credit decision can be taken on the basis of the CMA draft alone, because the credit process requires the approved rating and the analyst's approved memo.

sections.heading: Human-in-the-loop design and transparency
sections.text: Human oversight is exercised by the credit analyst, who reviews every generated paragraph with its source references and guardrail flags, and accepts, edits or rejects it; a memo cannot be submitted to the credit approval workflow while a paragraph is unreviewed or a red flag is unresolved. Criteria for intervention are defined in the user guide: any unsupported or flagged statement, any figure that cannot be traced to a source, and any content outside the section scope; the analyst can stop generation, regenerate or switch the assistant off for a memo, and the Use Case Owner can suspend the application for all users. The drafting panel informs users at first use and in every session that they interact with an AI system, and every generated paragraph is labelled 'AI-generated draft – Credit Memo Assistant v1.0 – generated on [date]' until the analyst approves it. The label is also written as machine-readable metadata (custom document properties ai_generated=true, application name and generation timestamp) into the memo document in the credit workflow. The credit approver sees an 'AI-assisted' indicator on memo sections drafted with CMA, and the reviewer's approval and edits are recorded in the audit log.

sections.heading: Methodology
sections.text: Four alternatives were assessed against documented criteria (regulatory requirements, data protection, faithfulness to sources, performance on the prompt development set, stability, transparency, cost and implementation effort). (A) An open-weight model fine-tuned on historical memos and hosted on premises: full control, but lower drafting quality in the prototype (groundedness 88.2% on PD-CMA) and a high risk of reproducing outdated memo content. (B) Retrieval-augmented generation with a hosted general-purpose model and strict grounding instructions: groundedness 96.1% on PD-CMA, no training on Bank data and traceable sources. (C) Template-based extraction without free-text generation: fully deterministic but limited to tables and standard phrases, with low time savings (estimated 15% against 45% for B). (D) A vendor credit memo software-as-a-service product: limited configurability of prompts and sources and insufficient documentation for validation at the time of assessment. Alternative B was selected; it is less transparent than C, which is justified by the materially better drafting coverage and is compensated by the additional controls of source references, grounding and numeric checks and mandatory human review.

sections.heading: Prompt design
sections.text: The system prompt (version sp-1.6) states the role and task of the model (drafting a section of a corporate credit memo for review by a credit analyst), the permitted sources (only the passages supplied in the prompt), the required output format (structured paragraphs with a source reference per statement, in the language of the memo), the instruction to answer only from the supplied sources and to state explicitly when information is not available, and the prohibited content (credit recommendations, ratings, judgements on the credit decision, personal opinions, speculation and personal data not in scope). Six section templates (st-1.4 to st-1.6) define for each memo section the retrieval queries, the required sub-headings and the key points expected by the memo template. Prompt variants were compared on the prompt development set; the final prompt reduced unsupported statements from 4.9% to 2.1% of statements compared with the first version, mainly by requiring a source reference per sentence and by explicit abstention instructions. System prompt, section templates, retrieval configuration, guardrail configuration and generation parameters are version-controlled in repository cma-platform and released only through the Bank's change management.

sections.heading: Retrieval design
sections.text: Retrieval uses hybrid search in Azure AI Search, combining BM25 keyword search and vector search on text-embedding-3-large embeddings by reciprocal rank fusion, followed by the semantic re-ranker. Queries are filtered on the obligor of the memo and on the user's entitlements, and restricted to documents with a document date within five years of the drafting date, with the most recent financial statements boosted. The top 8 passages per query are passed to the model, with a maximum of 24 passages per memo section (about 14,000 tokens). Retrieval quality was tested on the retrieval test set RT-CMA v1.1 (250 queries): recall of the relevant passages within the retrieved set (recall@8) is 93.6%, above the 90% minimum of AI-STD-710 §6.3, and 89.1% for German- and French-language documents. Chunking parameters (800 tokens with 100-token overlap) were selected over 400 and 1,200 tokens on the same test set (recall 91.8% and 92.4% respectively).

sections.heading: Source references and explainability
sections.text: Every generated paragraph includes references to the source passages used (document name, date and page), which are displayed as links next to the paragraph so that the reviewer can verify each statement against the source. At individual level, the explanation of a draft consists of the retrieved passages, the source references and the guardrail results, which are available to the analyst acting on the output; at global level, the design, the prompt logic and the evaluation results are described in this document and in the user guide. This level of explainability is proportionate to a drafting aid whose outputs are reviewed in full by a competent analyst.

sections.heading: Calibration
sections.text: The generation parameters are temperature 0.2, top_p 1.0, maximum output length 2,500 tokens per section and a fixed response format; the low temperature was chosen to reduce variability and unsupported content, as sensitivity tests showed a hallucination rate of 1.6% at temperature 0.2 against 3.4% at 0.7 on the golden set. All evaluations reported in EVD-20-EVAL were run at these production generation parameters, with the production system prompt, templates and guardrail configuration (configuration release cma-cfg-1.3.0). The parameters are part of the versioned configuration and can only be changed through change management with a regression evaluation. Guardrail thresholds were calibrated on the prompt development set: the grounding check flags statements with a support score below 0.80, which maximised the detection of unsupported statements (recall 94%) at an acceptable flag rate (7.8% of statements).

sections.heading: Guardrails
sections.text: Grounding check: each generated statement is verified against the retrieved passages by the groundedness detection of Azure AI Content Safety and an in-house entailment verifier; unsupported statements are highlighted in red and must be resolved by the reviewer before the draft can be approved. Numeric-claims check: every number in a draft (amounts, ratios, percentages and dates) is parsed and compared with the spread values and retrieved passages, with a tolerance of 0.5% relative for rounded amounts and exact matching for dates; ratios are recomputed with the documented ratio library (24 ratios), and any number that cannot be matched to a source value or a documented calculation is flagged to the reviewer. PII filter: inputs to the language model and outputs are screened for personal identifiers of natural persons (citizen service numbers, dates of birth, private addresses, private IBANs and passport numbers), which are masked in inputs and blocked in outputs, and every detection is logged. Prompt-injection and content checks: user inputs and retrieved passages are screened with Prompt Shields for direct and indirect prompt injection, and outputs with the content filters (medium severity threshold) and the out-of-scope classifier for harmful, discriminatory or out-of-scope content. Thresholds and actions (warn, mask, block) are documented in the guardrail configuration gr-1.3, and their effectiveness was tested in the evaluation (EVD-20-EVAL §10).

sections.heading: Performance
sections.text: The pre-production evaluation on the golden set GS-CMA v1.2 (320 cases, configuration cma-cfg-1.3.0, run EV-2027-05-18) measured groundedness, hallucination rate, numeric accuracy, completeness against the reference and correct abstention, as reported in EVD-20-EVAL. Groundedness was 96.8% of 9,870 factual statements, the hallucination rate 1.6% of outputs (5 of 320), numeric accuracy 99.2% of 11,480 values with all 92 incorrect values flagged by the numeric guardrail, completeness 91.4% of the reference key points and correct abstention 92% (23 of 25 cases); the thresholds of AI-STD-710 §8.3 for AI Risk Class Elevated are met. Performance is stable across samples: groundedness was 96.1% on the prompt development set and 96.3% on the out-of-time set, and it is reported per memo section, sector group and language. Correct abstention (92%) is below the internal target of 95%; the two failures concerned covenant compliance where a superseded certificate was retrieved, the cause was analysed, and the limitation is recorded as L-05 with the mitigation of document type correction and a date filter on certificates. The evaluation used an LLM-as-judge for statement support, calibrated against human labels on 150 cases with an agreement of 88.7% (EVD-20-EVAL §4).

sections.heading: Benchmarking
sections.text: CMA was benchmarked against the current manual process and against the alternative foundation models of section 4.2. In the shadow pilot, 12 analysts compared 214 CMA drafts with their own memo sections: 71% of CMA paragraphs were accepted with minor or no edits, 22% were edited substantially and 7% were rejected; drafting time for the six sections fell from a median of 3.9 hours to 2.1 hours per memo. On the golden set, the best alternative model reached groundedness of 95.1% and a hallucination rate of 2.8%, against 96.8% and 1.6% for gpt-4.1; the difference is explained by fewer unsupported statements in long financial tables. The Bank's own outcome testing on its credit files is the basis for the approval; provider benchmarks were used only for pre-selection.

sections.heading: Robustness, red-teaming and security
sections.text: Red-teaming was performed by the Information Security red team from 3 to 14 May 2027 with 420 attack prompts, covering direct and indirect prompt injection (including 120 manipulated annual reports), jailbreaking, extraction of the system prompt and confidential data, personal data leakage, biased or harmful content and use outside the approved boundaries. The block or neutralisation rate was 98.8%, no personal data leakage occurred, and no critical finding was raised; two medium findings (partial disclosure of the system prompt and one indirect injection that altered the tone of a paragraph) were remediated in guardrail configuration gr-1.3 and re-tested successfully. Red-teaming will be repeated at least annually and after each change of the foundation model version. Robustness against errors and data drift is addressed by the nightly DQ checks of the index, the monitoring of section 10, and the fallback to manual drafting when the service is unavailable.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivities of the evaluation metrics were computed on the golden set for the key design parameters. Temperature 0.7 instead of 0.2: hallucination rate 3.4% (+1.8 points) and groundedness 95.2%; top-k 5 instead of 8: completeness −4.3 points; chunk size 400 tokens: groundedness −0.6 points; removal of the abstention instruction: correct abstention falls from 92% to 56%; grounding threshold 0.70 instead of 0.80: detection of unsupported statements falls from 94% to 86%. The labelling guideline (EJ-CMA-01) was tested against the strictest alternative, which reduces groundedness from 96.8% to 95.9%. The results confirm that the chosen parameters are on the conservative side for faithfulness, and that the abstention instruction and the grounding threshold are the most important controls.

sections.heading: Assumptions and limitations
sections.text: The material assumptions are that the knowledge sources are complete and correct for the obligor at the drafting date, that the foundation model behaves in production as in the evaluation at the same pinned version and parameters, that the golden set is representative of production requests, and that analysts review drafts diligently. Each assumption was assessed for plausibility: completeness and correctness are supported by the DQ assessment of the index, model stability by version pinning and repeated runs, representativeness by the stratification of the golden set, and diligent review by the edit and rejection rates observed in the shadow pilot and by the monthly quality review. The main residual risk is automation bias, which is mitigated by mandatory paragraph-level review, visible flags and training.

sections.heading: Monitoring
sections.text: The monitoring plan MP-CMA v1.0, approved by the Model Owner on 28 May 2027 and to be reviewed by Model Validation – AI in the initial validation, defines GenAI-specific KPIs with thresholds approved by Model Risk Management on 1 June 2027. Monthly KPIs with green/amber/red thresholds are: groundedness on a sample of 50 production outputs labelled by two senior analysts (≥95% / 90–95% / <90%); hallucination rate on the same sample (≤2% / 2–5% / >5%); numeric values correct or flagged (100% / – / <100%); guardrail trigger rates per guardrail (within ±50% of the evaluation rate / beyond ±50% / beyond ±100%); reviewer edit and rejection rates (rejection ≤15% / 15–25% / >25%); user feedback (share of negative ratings ≤20% / 20–30% / >30%); availability (≥99.5% / 98–99.5% / <98%); and incidents (none / minor / any data leakage). Input drift is monitored through the PSI of memo section, sector and language against the golden set, with the default thresholds of MRM-STD-040 §5.2, and coverage as the share of memos drafted with CMA. KPIs are computed for the application as a whole and for each memo section, with results finalised within 30 calendar days after month-end by Wholesale Credit Analytics and reported to the Model Owner, the AI Governance Office and Credit Risk Management; a full monitoring report is produced annually as required for Tier 3 models. Each amber result is analysed by the Model Owner; a red result, or amber on the same KPI in two consecutive cycles, is notified to MRM, Model Validation and the AI Governance Office within five business days, followed within 60 calendar days by a root cause analysis and action plan (no action with justification, reconfiguration, restriction or suspension). The monitoring report shows each KPI with value, threshold, traffic light and trend over at least the last four cycles; monitoring code and samples are version controlled and results reproducible, and the plan is updated when CMA changes and reviewed at least annually.

sections.heading: Metrics
sections.text: Groundedness is the share of factual statements in the generated sections that are supported by the supplied sources. Hallucination rate is the share of outputs that contain at least one unsupported or incorrect material statement. Numeric accuracy is the share of numeric values (amounts, ratios, percentages and dates) that are correct, and the share of incorrect values flagged by the numeric guardrail is reported separately. Completeness is the share of key points of the reference answer covered by the draft, and correct abstention is the share of abstention cases in which CMA states that the information is not available instead of generating content. Thresholds for AI Risk Class Elevated are groundedness of at least 95%, a hallucination rate of at most 2% and 100% of numeric values correct or flagged; internal targets are completeness of at least 90% and correct abstention of at least 95%.

deficiencies.rationale: Materiality is scored Low (MDD §1.3), although criterion 6.2(d) requires at least Medium where model output is used in decisions on individual customers; the drafts feed the credit memo on which credit decisions are taken. With complexity Medium the §6.4 matrix yields Tier 2, not Tier 3.

mitigation.text: Re-score materiality with MRM; if Tier 2 is confirmed, apply the Model Approval Panel as approval authority, two-yearly validation and semi-annual monitoring reports.

deficiencies.rationale: The monthly second-line quality review is designed but only dry-run in the shadow pilot on 3% of drafts (7 of 214), below the minimum of 5% or 30 outputs; its effectiveness is not yet evidenced.

mitigation.text: Start the monthly quality review with at least 30 outputs in the first production month and report results to the Use Case Owner and MRM.

deficiencies.rationale: AI-generated text is marked in machine-readable form only as document properties of the memo file (MDD §2.4); the marking is lost when paragraphs are copied into other systems, so detectability is not ensured as far as technically feasible.

mitigation.text: Add paragraph-level machine-readable provenance tags in the credit workflow and block copy-out of unapproved AI-generated text.

deficiencies.rationale: The judge calibration reports 88.7% case-level agreement overall, but Model Validation's recomputation on the cases that humans labelled as containing a hallucination shows only 76% agreement; the judge under-detects hallucinations, so its use in repeated runs and sensitivities is not adequately calibrated for the metric that matters.

mitigation.text: Recalibrate the judge prompt on hallucination-positive cases (at least 85% agreement on a stratified sample) or replace judge-based repeated-run results by human labels.

deficiencies.rationale: The golden set is stratified on the 2024–2026 memo population, but production requests in the shadow pilot contain 19% multi-currency or non-EUR reporting groups against 4% in the golden set; groundedness on Model Validation's supplementary sample of such cases is 93.1%.

mitigation.text: Extend the golden set with at least 40 multi-currency group cases, re-run the evaluation and add a segment KPI for these cases to the monitoring plan.
